turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (NURSE): Morning, Mr Brennan. Pop your arm out there and I'll get a blood pressure before the doctor calls you.
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand, grand. Sure the bus in was a pure nightmare, twenty minutes stuck at the lights, and your man in front wouldn't budge an inch.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I told him let me drive. Does he listen? He does not. We nearly lost the appointment with the fussing.
[SEG0004] person_1 (NURSE): There we go. Blood pressure is one hundred and forty-six over eighty-eight, and your pulse is seventy-four. I'll leave that on the chart for the doctor.
[SEG0005] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tom, Mary, come on in and sit down. How have you been getting on since I saw you?

[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah I'm not too bad, doctor, only the arthritis in the right knee and the lower back are giving me fierce gyp. I'm in for the repeat script, and I was hoping you might give me something a bit stronger for the pain.
[SEG0007] person_4 (DOCTOR): Tell me about that pain in your own words. Where does it catch you, and how long has it been going on?

[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): The right knee mostly, and it travels up into the lower back. It's been five-ish years, ever since I packed in the bowling. Some mornings I can hardly get down the step into the garden.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): The roses are a disgrace because he won't go down to them. I bought a stick and it lives in the hall doing nothing.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): The stick makes me feel about a hundred. The paracetamol takes the edge off through the day, but it doesn't touch the pain at night.
[SEG0011] person_4 (DOCTOR): What tablets are you actually taking at the minute? Walk me through a normal day of them.

[SEG0012] person_2 (PATIENT): Paracetamol, two of the five-hundred milligram ones, four times in the day. Then the ibuprofen from the chemist, and the little stomach tablet, omeprazole, twenty milligrams every morning.
[SEG0013] person_4 (DOCTOR): Nurse, would you read what's on the pharmacy list, so we're not relying on memory?
[SEG0014] person_1 (NURSE): The chemist list says paracetamol one gram four times a day, ibuprofen four hundred milligrams three times a day, and omeprazole twenty milligrams once daily.

[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): Four hundred? Ah no, that's not right at all. I'm on the six hundred milligram ibuprofen, one tablet three times a day, and I take it with my food. Your one in the pharmacy said that herself last month.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I've seen the box in the press. It says six hundred, clear as day. I don't know where four hundred came out of.
[SEG0017] person_4 (DOCTOR): Right, so the list and the two of you don't agree, and I'm not going to guess a dose. We'll get the chemist to confirm it before anyone changes the strength.

[SEG0018] person_2 (PATIENT): Speaking of the chemist, the young lad behind the counter was three weeks in Spain. The heat, he said, was desperate, and the beer was dearer than a meal at home, and he wouldn't stop talking about the pool.
[SEG0019] person_4 (DOCTOR): Ha, we'll leave Spain for a quieter day. Any other tablets at all, even ones you tried and stopped?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): I used to take codeine tablets years ago, but they made me dopey, so I stopped them. Nothing else, prescribed or out of the shop.
[SEG0021] person_4 (DOCTOR): Any dizziness, or pain in the chest, when you're up and about?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): No, nothing like that. I'm grand that way. No dizziness, and no pain in the chest.
[SEG0023] person_4 (DOCTOR): What about the stomach? Any heartburn or burning with the ibuprofen?
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): No, not a bother. Sure that's what the omeprazole is for.
[SEG0025] person_4 (DOCTOR): And how are the bowels and the waterworks? Any trouble there at all?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): No, all grand on that front. Regular as anything, touch wood.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His mother, God rest her, was crippled with the arthritis. I keep saying it runs in the family, not that he wants to hear it.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): She was, aye. I packed in the post office when I turned sixty-six. Never smoked in my life, and it's only the odd pint of a Saturday, nothing wild.
[SEG0029] person_4 (DOCTOR): And you're at home with Mary, I take it?
[SEG0030] person_2 (PATIENT): I am, yeah. She does the driving now, whether I like it or not. Boss of the house.
[SEG0031] person_4 (DOCTOR): When you had bloods done, what did they tell you? I'm thinking of the kidneys, with the ibuprofen.

[SEG0032] person_2 (PATIENT): They did them in the spring, and they said the kidney function was borderline. They never gave me a number, just borderline, and to be careful with the anti-inflammatories.
[SEG0033] person_4 (DOCTOR): That's worth knowing, even without a figure. I'm not keen on adding a stronger painkiller on top of a borderline kidney result and a dose we can't settle.
[SEG0034] person_2 (PATIENT): So you're thinking no? My neighbour Dessie got tramadol off his own doctor and he says it changed his life. I had my hopes up, I'll be honest.

[SEG0035] person_4 (DOCTOR): I hear you, and I'm sorry to disappoint you. I'm not going to prescribe tramadol or anything stronger today. Staying with the paracetamol, and the ibuprofen only once we know the strength, is the safer plan.
[SEG0036] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, that's a pity now. The nights are the killer. I have to lift the leg out of the bed with both hands, like an old yoke.
[SEG0037] person_4 (DOCTOR): When you stand up out of the chair, or out of bed, do you feel steady on your feet?
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I do go a bit swimmy in the head if I stand up quick. Just for a second or two. I said no to the dizziness earlier, but that isn't quite true.
[SEG0039] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He grabs the back of the chair, I've watched him. Then he pretends he was only fixing the cushion.

[SEG0040] person_4 (DOCTOR): Thanks for telling me straight. That light-headedness when you stand is worth having on the table, and it's another reason I'd rather not start an opioid. I'll have a look at the knee while you're here.
[SEG0041] person_4 (DOCTOR): The right knee is swollen, and it creaks when you bend it, but it's not hot and it's not red. You get to about ninety degrees and then it stops you.

[SEG0042] person_2 (PATIENT): The knee blows up if I walk down to the shops. And the creaking, Mary says she can hear it from the kitchen, which is gas, because she has the radio on full blast anyway.
[SEG0043] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Never mind the radio. He skips the middle ibuprofen half the time when he's out pottering, so don't be writing down that he takes it three times a day religiously.
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): I do take it. Well, most days. If I'm in the garden I might forget the lunchtime one, I'll give you that much.
[SEG0045] person_4 (DOCTOR): Okay, so the three times a day is a bit hit and miss. Any allergies to medicines, Tom, before we go on?
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): No, none. Never had a rash or anything off a tablet.
[SEG0047] person_4 (DOCTOR): Grand. My impression is this is your osteoarthritis flaring, the same knee and the same back, not some new illness landing on you.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): So what do we actually do, then? I'm still sore, and the match is on tonight so I can't be up and down to the kettle the whole time.

[SEG0049] person_4 (DOCTOR): Keep the paracetamol at one gram four times a day, take the ibuprofen with food, and only once the chemist confirms whether it's four hundred or six hundred. Don't start any stronger painkiller, and don't borrow Dessie's tramadol.
[SEG0050] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll send you for a fresh kidney blood test this week, seeing as they only called it borderline in the spring and we've no number to go on.
[SEG0051] person_1 (NURSE): I can book that with the blood clinic for Thursday, if Thursday suits the two of you.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): Thursday's grand, sure that's pension day anyway, we'll be in town. Will the dose get sorted as well, or are we leaving that hanging?
[SEG0053] person_4 (DOCTOR): Bring the ibuprofen box to the chemist this week and ask them to ring us with the strength on the label. I'm not changing it until that's clear.
[SEG0054] person_4 (DOCTOR): I'll see you back here in six weeks with the blood result. If the knee turns hot or red, or the dizziness gets worse, come back sooner and don't wait the six weeks.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks, alright. I'll try the blessed stick, I suppose, if it keeps herself quiet about the roses.
[SEG0056] person_4 (DOCTOR): Fair play to you. Mind yourselves on the bus home, and we'll go through those bloods when I see you.

spec.situation: Routine repeat-prescription review at a small clinic with a pharmacy technician present; patient wants a stronger painkiller; tablet names and doses are discussed in detail, one dose is read from the pharmacy list and differs from the patient's own; doctor declines the stronger medicine.
features: test_result_recalled: the patient reports an old test or result ('they said it was borderline'); recorded as reported history/investigation only as far as said, not as a confirmed value.
disputed_numbers: the nurse reads a value and the patient or relative disagrees or remembers another (a dose, a weight, a BP). Keep both and record an uncertainty.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.

spoken_numbers: doses, vitals and durations are spoken as words or sloppy speech ('a hundred and two point five', 'one-forty over ninety', 'five-ish years', 'twenty milligram'); the label writes them normally (102.5, 140/90, 20 mg) and does not turn vague ones into exact ones.
